title: Ghost of Lessons Past Pt 2
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Brien looks back at two elaborate lessons from his early career, a staged crime scene with fingerprinting for Legal Studies and a rainbow-parachute experience of synesthesia for Psychology, which looked like gold-standard engagement. His reality check is that students learned nothing useful, the content was never referred to again, and he burned hours of preparation. Experiential activities, he argues, can teach the wrong lessons and produce weak transfer, while the lesson collapses once the novel stimulus is gone. He now would explicitly teach the concept, run checks for understanding and use spaced and interleaved practice. His claim is that explicit instruction is engaging in a different and more durable way, because success builds intrinsic motivation and confidence. The confessional framing makes the argument for explicit teaching persuasive and personal.
points: Visible busyness and engagement during a lesson are not evidence of learning, and a lesson that impresses observers can still teach nothing.
Experiential 'hook' activities risk teaching the wrong lesson and give weak transfer when students only experience one case of a concept.
The replacement sequence is to explicitly teach the idea and then run repeated checks for understanding using applied case studies.
Time spent on novelty is time taken from spaced practice and interleaving that would better prepare students.
Explicit instruction builds intrinsic motivation and self-confidence through a positive feedback loop of success.
quotes: Now if you were on a learning walk and came by my classroom that day you would’ve seen a hive of engagement, students fingerprinting each other, dusting for prints, causing unspeakable levels of mess. If any leaders were walking past they honestly would’ve used it as an example of the gold standard of teaching.

Students did not learn a single thing useful to their legal studies education during that hour of class. Nor was anything we did in that lesson ever referred to in class for the remainder of the year.

I certainly would do things differently. I would first explicitly teach what the Standard of Proof is, then simply conduct a range of Checks for Understanding about what the Standard of Proof is and how it applies.

Experiential learning despite being ‘fun’ for students can often lead to the wrong lessons being learned. I had spent a relatively enormous amount of time having the students experience only one kind of sense being triggered when the truth is that it could be one of many and therefore by relying solely on this experiential learning with no other examples or checks for understanding the students were likely to have weak transfer of the knowledge to other scenarios or problems.

Could either of the above be used as a hook to engage students? Sure, but the reality here is that I lost countless hours of learning time with these students where I could’ve been conducting spaced practice and interleaved learning and setting them up far better for the future.
In both of the above activities, once the novel stimulus was gone I had completely lost the students and the rest of the lesson was a complete write-off. Short. Sharp. Precise.
